entries.clue: Pipe, a help to the vicar (12)

blocks.note: a long-stemmed clay tobacco pipe, named after parish officers
a lay officer elected to assist the parish priest

annotation.surface: A parishioner offering the vicar a hand, perhaps with the plumbing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pipe' tempts you towards plumbing or music; it is the long clay pipe named after the parish officers said to have smoked it.
annotation.definitionFit: A churchwarden is both a long clay pipe and a lay assistant in an Anglican parish.

entries.clue: US money put in the post, we hear (4)

indicatorNotes.we hear: what we hear is the sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: a letter put in the post has been sent

annotation.surface: Someone mailing dollars through the post.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put in the post' is a whole phrase standing for one past-tense word, and only its sound is used.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the smallest American coin, one hundredth of a dollar.

entries.clue: Modernises what is past due for review (7)

indicatorNotes.for review: to review is to go over again, here rearranging the letters

annotation.surface: An overdue report or bill being brought up to date.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Past due' reads as one phrase meaning overdue, which hides that its seven letters are simply the answer rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: To update something is to modernise it.

entries.clue: Empty plain (5)

blocks.note: a verb here, as when you empty a room of furniture
an adjective here, meaning obvious or easy to see

annotation.walkthrough: Read together the two words sound like a bare landscape; split them, and 'Empty' is a verb while 'plain' is the adjective meaning obvious.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms from different parts of speech: the verb for removing everything, and the adjective for what is evident.

entries.clue: Women's organisation has the right to fade (6)

annotation.surface: A women's group asserting its entitlement to slip quietly into the background.
annotation.walkthrough: The WI (Women's Institute) is a long-established British community organisation for women, famous for jam and Jerusalem; 'has' just sits the pieces side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, drawn from plants that dry up and lose their colour.

entries.clue: System for Reg and I to go ahead of troops (7)

indicatorNotes.to go ahead of: REG and I come before the troops

annotation.surface: Two officers marching out in front of their soldiers under a set plan.
annotation.walkthrough: Reg reads as a man's name and is taken letter for letter; the military picture also fits the answer's echo of 'regiment'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually for a set routine of diet, exercise or treatment.

entries.clue: Prophesy pair will leave order (5)

indicatorNotes.will leave: the pair's letters depart from the word

annotation.surface: A foretelling that a couple is about to walk out of a religious order.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a monastic community the pair are quitting; it is the definition, a decree.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a command issued by someone in authority.

entries.clue: After last month, prophet turned up with orders (7)

indicatorNotes.After: the second piece comes after the month
indicatorNotes.turned up: in a down clue, reading upwards reverses the word

blocks.note: a seer is a prophet; turned up it reads REES

annotation.surface: A prophet arriving in January bearing commandments.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Last month' could be November if read as 'the month just gone'; here it is the last month of the year.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the plural noun: formal rulings handed down by authority.

entries.clue: Naturist holds note as a gentle reminder (5)

indicatorNotes.holds: the naturist's word keeps the note inside it

annotation.surface: A naturist leaving a little written note as a prompt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Note' reads as a written memo in a clue about reminders; it is one of the musical notes A to G.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: a light push with the elbow, extended to any gentle prompt.

entries.clue: Slogan of game family (3,4)

blocks.note: tag is a children's chasing game

annotation.surface: The catchphrase of some game-playing family.
annotation.walkthrough: Tag is the playground chasing game, and 'family' is a line of descent.
annotation.definitionFit: A tagline is a catchy slogan, as used in advertising.

entries.clue: Travelling to resort, tram needs part that fires (7,5)

indicatorNotes.Travelling: the letters are on the move

annotation.surface: A tram on its way to a seaside resort needing a spare part.
annotation.walkthrough: The tram and the part that fires both belong to the engine story, so the anagram hides well.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: the electric motor that cranks an engine until it fires.

entries.clue: Ruler for each in capital returning (7)

annotation.surface: A ruler coming back to his capital to see each subject.
annotation.walkthrough: Rome is the capital that fits both the letters and the surface: the city of the emperors.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, specifically the sovereign of an empire.

entries.clue: His map was ripped in unfortunate accident (6)

indicatorNotes.was ripped: a ripped map is torn apart, its letters scattered

annotation.surface: Someone's map getting torn by accident.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder is the first two words exactly; the torn map in the surface is itself a small mishap.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, for a minor piece of bad luck.

entries.clue: Camera I adapted for the country (7)

indicatorNotes.adapted: the letters are altered into a new form

annotation.surface: A traveller converting their camera to work abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: The lone I must join CAMERA in the fodder; 'the country' is vague on purpose, leaving the letters to decide.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the United States, commonly called America, is one example of a country.

entries.clue: Nervous near the brink? (2,4)

blocks.note: the same words taken literally, positioned at a drop

annotation.surface: Someone jittery standing close to a cliff.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading as a literal one: standing at the edge.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for tense, which also reads literally as placed right at a border or precipice.

entries.clue: Tail went up by flower (3,4)

blocks.note: to tail someone is to dog them, follow closely

annotation.surface: A dog's tail lifting as it passes a flower bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tail' pictures a wagging dog's tail, and the answer does have a dog in it, but the word is a verb: to follow.
annotation.definitionFit: The dog rose is a wild climbing rose with pink or white flowers.

entries.clue: Advice to first of people is excellent (3-3)

blocks.note: a tip is a piece of advice

annotation.surface: Praise for tips offered to the leading figure of the people.
annotation.walkthrough: The little word 'to' is used letter for letter rather than as a link.
annotation.definitionFit: Tip-top means first-rate, excellent.

entries.clue: Branch of medicine involving lime pie - goody! (12)

indicatorNotes.involving: the letters are tangled up together

annotation.surface: A medical specialism that somehow involves dessert, to someone's delight.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation 'goody!' looks like pure decoration, but all five of its letters are needed in the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Epidemiology is the branch of medicine that studies how diseases spread in populations.

entries.clue: Get used to being in river (5)

blocks.note: the Ure is a Yorkshire river, a crossword regular

annotation.surface: Someone acclimatising to cold water by swimming in a river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction but is taken as the word itself, placed before the river.
annotation.definitionFit: To inure yourself to something is to get used to it, especially something unpleasant.

entries.clue: Enjoys hawk film that follows large one (5)

indicatorNotes.that follows: the film comes after the other pieces

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as on clothing sizes
Kes (1969) is Ken Loach's film about a boy and his kestrel

annotation.surface: A film-goer who enjoys watching birds of prey on screen.
annotation.walkthrough: KES is a British classic: a Yorkshire boy trains a kestrel, a small hawk.
annotation.definitionFit: To like something is to enjoy it.

entries.clue: Piste runners kiss unexpectedly (4)

indicatorNotes.unexpectedly: the letters turn up in a surprising order

annotation.surface: A stolen kiss between skiers on the slopes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Runners' pictures people; it means the parts that run along the snow, as a sledge has runners.
annotation.definitionFit: Skis are the long runners strapped to the feet on a piste.

entries.clue: Locum, unrestricted, takes register to eye specialist (7)

indicatorNotes.unrestricted: without its borders, so the outer letters go

blocks.note: LOCUM loses its outer letters L and M

annotation.surface: A stand-in doctor with free rein sending patients to the eye clinic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unrestricted' reads as free to practise; it means the word's boundaries come off.
annotation.definitionFit: An oculist is an old term for an eye doctor.

entries.clue: Nothing is about in outer limits of Kilmarnock but a booth (5)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' means surrounding, so IS is placed around the O
indicatorNotes.in: that goes inside the outer letters
indicatorNotes.outer limits of: take only the first and last letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Kilmarnock
used as printed, wrapped round the O

annotation.surface: The edge of Kilmarnock, a Scottish town, having nothing there but a single kiosk.
annotation.walkthrough: Kilmarnock is a town in Ayrshire, Scotland; only its first and last letters are used.
annotation.definitionFit: A kiosk is a small booth selling papers or snacks.

entries.clue: Cyclists' gear? (5-7)

blocks.note: literally, those who push pedals round; also the name of a garment
the surface pushes bicycle gears; the setter means clothing

annotation.walkthrough: 'Gear' hints at a bike's gears, but it means clothing: pedal-pushers are calf-length trousers first worn for cycling, and cyclists are literally pedal-pushers.
annotation.definitionFit: Pedal-pushers are cropped trousers originally designed to stay clear of a bicycle chain.
